title: Thermodynamic Potentials
text:
Starting with:
\[
dU = T dS - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r \tag{1}
\]
Notice that Equation 1 is now composed entirely of state functions. This introduces internal energy (\(U\)) as a thermodynamic potential, indicating that \(U\) is fundamentally a function of entropy, volume, and the number of moles. While it is mathematically possible to express internal energy using temperature and volume instead, the resulting equation loses its compact elegance—a natural mathematical framing referred to as a canonical relationship.
However, applying Equation 1 directly requires functional models that relate variables like \(T\), \(P\), and \(\mu_i\) back to \(S\), \(V\), and \(\bar{n}\). Because such models are rare and typically impractical for standard chemical engineering applications, it is often more useful to mathematically eliminate entropy as an independent variable. We do this using an operation called a Legendre transformation:
\[
dU - d(TS) = T dS - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r - d(TS)
\]
Expanding the differential \(d(TS)\) yields:
\[
d(U - TS) = T dS - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r - T dS - S dT
\]
Canceling out the \(T dS\) terms gives us the transformed potential:
\[
d(U - TS) = -S dT - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r \tag{2}
\]
We might recognize the left side of Equation 2 as the definition of the Helmholtz free energy (\(A\)):
\[
A \equiv U - TS \tag{3}
\]
If you haven’t encountered Helmholtz free energy before, do not worry; the key takeaway at this stage is recognizing that we have defined a new property (distinct from internal energy) that acts as a canonical function of temperature, volume, and composition (\(\bar{n}\)):
\[
dA = -S dT - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r \tag{4}
\]
From a multivariable calculus perspective, this total differential allows us to extract the following partial derivatives:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial T} \right)_{V, \bar{n}} = -S \tag{5}
\]
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} = -P \tag{6}
\]
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T, V, n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i \tag{7}
\]
For our current purposes, Equation 6 is the most crucial. If we have a pressure-explicit equation of state—meaning we know pressure as a function of \(T\), \(V\), and \(\bar{n}\)—we can easily calculate differences in Helmholtz free energy by integrating:
\[
A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = \int_{V_R}^{V} \left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} dV = -\int_{V_R}^{V} P dV \tag{8}
\]
An even more commonly recognized potential is the Gibbs free energy. We can derive it by applying another Legendre transformation to Equation 4, this time swapping out volume in favor of pressure as our independent variable:
\[
dA + d(PV) = -S dT - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r + d(PV)
\]
Expanding this and substituting our previous enthalpy definitions yields the fundamental relation for Gibbs free energy (\(G\)):
\[
d(U - TS + PV) \equiv d(H - TS) \equiv d(G) = -S dT + V dP + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r \tag{9}
\]
Although Gibbs energy is ideal for constant T and P problems, it is clumsy as an overarching computational framework. Most equations of state solve for P(T, V), not V(T, P), because volume is multi-valued across phase transitions—such as water at 100°C and 1atm, where liquid and vapor share identical pressures. Practical computational thermodynamics therefore depends on working with other potentials, notably Helmholtz energy, to avoid root-finding ambiguities.

title: Thermodynamic Potentials
section: Summary of Potentials for Simple Systems
text:
Summary of Potentials for Simple Systems

Helmholtz free energy, \(A\)
Differential form
\[
dA = -S dT - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r
\]
Derivatives

\(\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial T} \right)_{V,\bar{n}} = -S\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T,\bar{n}} = -P\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V,n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i\)



Gibbs free energy, \(G = A + PV\)
Differential form
\[
dG = -S dT + V dP + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r
\]
Derivatives

\(\left( \frac{\partial G}{\partial T} \right)_{P,\bar{n}} = -S\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial G}{\partial P} \right)_{T,\bar{n}} = V\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P,n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i\)



Enthalpy, \(H = A + PV + TS\)
Differential form
\[
dH = T dS + V dP + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r
\]
Derivatives

\(\left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial S} \right)_{P,\bar{n}} = T\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial P} \right)_{S,\bar{n}} = V\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,P,n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i\)



Internal energy, \(U = A + TS\)
Differential form
\[
dU = T dS - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r
\]
Derivatives

\(\left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial S} \right)_{V,\bar{n}} = T\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial V} \right)_{S,\bar{n}} = -P\)
\(\left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,V,n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i\)

Also, as mentioned above, the chemical potential can be written in terms of any of the potentials:
\[
\mu_i = \left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,V,n_{k \neq i}} = \left( \frac{\partial G}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T,P,n_{k \neq i}} = \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,P,n_{k \neq i}} = \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial n_i} \right)_{S,V,n_{k \neq i}} \tag{10}
\]

title: Thermodynamic Potentials
section: Why Gibbs Energy Is Difficult to Integrate Directly from an EOS
text:
Why Gibbs Energy Is Difficult to Integrate Directly from an EOS
While Gibbs free energy might feel more intuitive when dealing with constant temperature (\(T\)) and pressure (\(P\)) problems like phase equilibrium and reactions, directly calculating \(G(T, P, n)\) by integrating an equation of state presents significant mathematical hurdles.
The fundamental differential expression for \(G\) requires us to integrate volume with respect to pressure:
\[
\Delta G = \int V(T, P, n) dP
\]
The problem is that standard equations of state (like cubic EOS models) are fundamentally cubic in volume (\(V\)). This means it is impossible to algebraically rearrange them into a clean, single-valued explicit function of the form \(V = f(T, P, n)\).
Furthermore, if you are working within the two-phase region, the function \(V(P)\) becomes multi-valued—it simultaneously yields roots for the liquid phase, the vapor phase, and a mechanically unstable state. This multi-valued nature makes integrating directly along the \(dP\) path incredibly cumbersome.
Helmholtz energy (\(A\)), however, offers a trivial workaround. Integrating the expression \(-P(T, V, n) dV\) is straightforward because pressure (\(P\)) is explicitly and uniquely defined as an algebraic function of volume (\(V\)) across the entire thermodynamic domain. Once you have calculated \(A(T, V, n)\), you can instantly recover the Gibbs energy simply by adding the \(PV\) term.

1. Volume Is Not a Mathematical Function of Pressure
Strictly speaking, for a mathematical relationship to be considered a true function (\(y = f(x)\)), every input must map to exactly one output.
However, for fluids operating below their critical point, defining the temperature (\(T\)) and pressure (\(P\)) does not guarantee a unique volume:
Phase Coexistence: Think about water boiling at 100°C and 1 atm. At those exact conditions, the system could be a purely saturated liquid (\(V_L \approx 0.00104\text{ m}^3\text{/kg}\)), a purely saturated vapor (\(V_V \approx 1.673\text{ m}^3\text{/kg}\)), or any two-phase mixture in between.
Analytic Equations of State: When using models like Peng-Robinson or Soave-Redlich-Kwong, setting \(T\) and \(P\) within the two-phase envelope results in a cubic polynomial that produces three real roots:

A small root (representing the liquid-like volume).
A large root (representing the vapor-like volume).
An intermediate root that is mechanically unstable (where \((\partial P / \partial V)_T > 0\)).

Because \(V(P)\) is multi-valued in these scenarios, it is impossible to express it as a clean, explicit, single-valued algebraic function of the form \(V = f(T, P)\).


2. The Computational Bottleneck with Gibbs Energy
To compute changes in Gibbs energy directly from mechanical variables, the fundamental math requires us to integrate volume over pressure
\[
\Delta G = \int V(T, P) dP
\]
Because volume is multi-valued across phase transitions, trying to evaluate \(\int V dP\) forces us to trace theoretical paths through unstable van der Waals loops or manually enforce equal-area Maxwell constructions. This complexity makes direct path integration of Gibbs energy highly impractical for computational models.


3. Why the Helmholtz Framework Resolves This
While volume is not a single-valued function of pressure, the reverse is incredibly convenient: pressure is always a single-valued function of volume.
\[
P = f(T, V, n)
\]
Because of this mathematical reality, if you specify the temperature (\(T\)) and volume (\(V\)), calculating the pressure requires only a single, straightforward evaluation of the equation of state (EOS). This leads to two major advantages in computational thermodynamics:
Seamless Integration: The integral used to calculate the residual Helmholtz free energy is continuous, single-valued, and analytically integrable across the entire fluid domain (smoothly covering both liquid and vapor phases without unstable loops):
\[
A^{res}(T, V) = -\int_{\infty}^{V} \left( P - \frac{RT}{V} \right) dV
\]
How Thermodynamics Engines Actually Work: Because of these mathematical advantages, modern computational thermodynamics engines compute all their core variables—including residual properties, fugacity coefficients (\(\ln \phi_i\)), and chemical potentials—entirely within the \((T, V)\) Helmholtz domain. When a user actually requests a result at a specific constant temperature and pressure (\(T, P\)), the solver first finds the volumetric roots (\(V\)) at that given pressure, evaluates \(A(T, V)\), and then simply recovers the Gibbs free energy algebraically at the very end:
\[
G = A + PV
\]

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
text: First Law of Thermodynamics for a closed system, starting from the universal principle of conservation of energy.

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
text:
1. Total Energy Conservation
Because the universe is isolated, the sum of all energy changes must equal zero: energy cannot be created or destroyed:
\[\Delta(E_{kin} + E_{pot} + U)_{Sys} + \Delta(E_{kin} + E_{pot} + U)_{Surr} = 0\tag{1}\]
The universe is divided into two parts: the System (Sys, the region of interest) and the Surroundings (Surr, everything else).
The total energy of any body or region consists of:

\(E_{kin}\): macroscopic kinetic energy (movement of the center of mass)
\(E_{pot}\): macroscopic potential energy (position in external fields, like gravity).
\(U\): microscopic internal energy (molecular vibrations, rotations, electronic states, intermolecular forces)

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
text:
2. Practical Approximations and Boundary Transfers
\[\Delta(U)_{Sys} = -\Delta(E_k + E_p + U)_{Surr} = Q + W\tag{2}\]
Neglecting macroscopic motion of the system: In most chemical and physical systems (e.g., a beaker, reactor, or piston), the system as a whole does not undergo changes in bulk elevation or bulk velocity, meaning \(\Delta E_{kin} = 0\) and \(\Delta E_{pot} = 0\). Therefore, the only energy change occurring inside the system is internal energy: \(\Delta U_{\text{Sys}}\).
Energy transfer across the boundary: Modeling the entire surrounding universe is practically impossible. Instead of tracking what happens inside the surroundings, thermodynamics tracks the energy crossing the boundary between the system and surroundings:

\(Q\) (Heat): Energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
\(W\) (Work): Energy transferred through mechanical, electrical, or expansion forces.

Under this sign convention (the standard IUPAC convention), heat added to the system (\(Q > 0\)) and work done on the system (\(W > 0\)) increase its internal energy.

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
text:
3. Differential Form
\[dU = \delta Q + \delta W\tag{3}\]
When focusing strictly on the system, the “\(Sys\)” subscript is dropped for simplicity.
Expressed for an infinitesimal process:
\(dU\) is an exact differential, indicating that internal energy \(U\) is a state function (depends only on the current state, not the path taken).
\(\delta Q\) and \(\delta W\) use the inexact differential symbol (\(\delta\) or sometimes \(d\)), signifying that heat and work are path functions (they depend on the specific path taken between states.
If we limit to boundary work:
\[
\delta W_{Bound} = -P dV \tag{4}
\]






Note



Physical meaning. Represents mechanical expansion or compression work exerted across a movable system boundary (such as a piston).
Sign convention.

When a system expands (\(\Delta V > 0\)), it does work on the surroundings, spending its own internal energy; hence \(\delta W < 0\).
When a system is compressed (\(\Delta V < 0\)), the surroundings do work on the system, adding energy; hence \(\delta W > 0\).
The negative sign ensures consistency with the standard IUPAC convention where energy entering the system is positive.



Substitute (4) into (3):
\[
dU = \delta Q - P dV \tag{5}
\]






Note



Substituting \(\delta W = -P dV\) into \(dU = \delta Q + \delta W\) limits the mechanical interactions strictly to reversible boundary work, neglecting other forms like shaft work, electrical work, or surface tension.
Internal energy therefore changes through two primary pathways: heat transfer (\(\delta Q\)) and mechanical volume changes (\(-P dV\)).

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
section: 4. Extension to Variable Composition and Open Systems
text:
4. Extension to Variable Composition and Open Systems

4.1. Functional Dependence of Internal Energy
For a closed system of fixed composition, internal energy depends only on two independent extensive state variables—typically entropy \(S\) and volume \(V\):
\[
U = U(S, V)
\]
If matter can cross the boundary, or if chemical reactions/phase changes alter the amounts of species present, \(U\) must also depend explicitly on the mole numbers of each constituent species \(n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k\):
\[
U = U(S, V, n_1, n_2, \dots, n_k)
\]


4.2. Total Differential via Multivariable Calculus
Taking the total differential of \(U(S, V, \{n_r\})\) using the chain rule gives:
\[
dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V, n} dS + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_{S, n} dV + \sum_r \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial n_r}\right)_{S, V, n_{j \neq r}} dn_r
\]
From classical closed-system thermodynamics:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V, n} = T
\]
\[
\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_{S, n} = -P
\]


4.3. Definition of Chemical Potential
The partial derivative with respect to composition is defined as the chemical potential of species \(r\):
\[
\mu_r \equiv \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial n_r}\right)_{S, V, n_{j \neq r}}
\]
Substituting these definitions into the total differential yields:
\[
dU = T dS - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r \tag{6}
\]
For a reversible heat transfer where \(\delta Q_{rev} = T dS\), this directly becomes:
\[
dU = \delta Q - P dV + \sum_r \mu_r dn_r
\]






Note



Physical reason. If molecules are added to or removed from a system, they carry internal energy with them (chemical bond energies, rotational/vibrational modes, and intermolecular potential energy with neighboring molecules). Even if heat transfer is zero (\(\delta Q = 0\)) and the volume remains rigid (\(dV = 0\)), adding particles changes the total internal energy of the system. The summation term \(\sum_r \mu_r dn_r\) directly tracks that energetic change.

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
text:
5. The Second Law
The Second Law of Thermodynamics is often more conceptually challenging for students than the First Law. At its core, the Second Law can be summarized simply: the total entropy of the universe can never decrease.
\[
\Delta S_{\text{Sys}} + \Delta S_{\text{Surr}} \ge 0 \tag{7}
\]
While the First Law focuses on the conservation of energy, the Second Law dictates the direction of natural processes. For example, the First Law alone doesn’t rule out liquid water spontaneously freezing above its melting temperature; it only dictates the energy balance if such a process occurred. By introducing an inequality, the Second Law expressly forbids certain processes, establishing what is physically possible.
It is important to note that the Second Law does not prevent the entropy of a specific system or its surroundings from decreasing individually—it only requires that their combined total cannot decrease. Furthermore, to make this principle practical, we need a way to actually calculate entropy changes. This is where the concept of a reversible process is introduced. In a purely reversible process, the total entropy change of the universe (system plus surroundings) is exactly zero, turning the inequality of Eq. 7 into an equality. This allows us to define the differential change in entropy mathematically as:
\[
dS \equiv \left( \frac{\delta Q}{T} \right)_{\text{rev}} \tag{8}
\]

title: From the First Law to the Fundamental Relation
section: 6. Why State Functions, Not Path Functions
text:
6. Why State Functions, Not Path Functions
By combining the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics, we replace path functions (Q, W) with exact differentials (state functions: Internal Energy, Temperature, Entropy, Pressure, and Volume) to create the Fundamental Thermodynamic Relation (Equation 6).
Path functions are not practically “bad”—in fact, heat and work are exactly what engineers care about because that is what we pay for in the real world (e.g., fuel for heat, electricity for work). However, from a mathematical and analytical standpoint, path functions are incredibly difficult to work with compared to state functions for three main reasons:

6.1. The “Memory” Problem
To calculate a path function like work (\(W = \int P dV\)), you cannot just look at the starting and ending volumes. You must know the exact history of how the expansion happened. Did the pressure drop linearly? Exponentially? Was there friction? Was it done infinitely slowly (reversible) or violently (irreversible)? If you do not know the exact mathematical function of the path taken, you cannot solve the integral.
State functions, however, have no memory. To find the change in internal energy (\(\Delta U\)), you only need simple subtraction: \(\Delta U = U_{final} - U_{initial}\). You do not need to know anything about the process itself.


6.2. You Cannot Put Path Functions in a Table
Because state functions (\(P, V, T, U, S, H\)) only depend on the current physical condition of the system, we can tabulate them. This is why we have Steam Tables and thermodynamic databases (like CoolProp or NIST). You can look up the exact internal energy or entropy of water at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) and \(1\text{ atm}\).
You can never create a table for “Heat” or “Work” because a system does not contain heat or work. They are actions, not properties.


6.3. The Thermodynamic “Cheat Code”
Real-world processes are almost always irreversible (they happen quickly, with friction, turbulence, and heat loss). Calculating \(\delta Q\) or \(\delta W\) for an irreversible process is mathematically messy, sometimes impossible.
Because state functions only care about the endpoints, they unlock a massive analytical loophole: You can calculate the change for a chaotic, irreversible process by inventing an imaginary, perfectly reversible path between the same two states.

If you want to know \(\Delta U\) for a messy explosion in a cylinder, you don’t need to model the explosion’s path.
You just look at the state before the explosion (\(T_1, P_1\)) and the state after the explosion (\(T_2, P_2\)).
You use the fundamental relation (\(dU = T dS - P dV\)) over an easy, idealized path to find the difference between those two states.
Because \(U\) is a state function, the \(\Delta U\) you calculate for the imaginary easy path is 100% identical to the \(\Delta U\) of the messy real-world explosion.

title: About
text: Notes on phase behaviour, equations of state, and the numerics underneath them, by Khanh Vu.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
Copy a formula out of ChatGPT and paste it into Word and you get one of three disappointments: a picture you cannot edit, a line of raw \frac{a}{b}, or a row of mangled symbols. None of them is a Word equation.
That is not Word being obtuse. The formula on screen was never an equation, and the thing Word wants is a format no chat site produces. This post is about what sits on each side of that gap, and what has to go on the clipboard to bridge it.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
section: A formula on a web page is not a formula
text:
A formula on a web page is not a formula
Nothing in a web page is an equation. A chat site renders math with a JavaScript library, almost always MathJax or KaTeX, and what lands in the DOM is one of:

SVG. MathJax’s SVG output draws each glyph as vector paths. Visually perfect, semantically nothing. Copy it and you have copied a drawing.
Styled HTML. MathJax’s CommonHTML output and KaTeX build the formula from spans with careful CSS. What looks like a fraction bar is a <span> with a border.
An image. A few sites still render server-side to PNG.

The visual layer is a dead end in all three cases. What rescues the situation is that the libraries also leave the semantics in the page, out of sight. KaTeX emits a hidden MathML copy next to the visual one; MathJax ships an Assistive MathML extension that, in its own words, “inserts hidden MathML for the usual output renderers.” And MathML has a slot for the original source:
<annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{RT}{V_m - b}</annotation>
So the LaTeX you typed is usually still on the page, one layer down. Finding it reliably is harder than it sounds: the attribute names, the element structure and even whether the hidden copy exists at all vary by renderer, by renderer version, and by how a given site configures it. But the principle holds everywhere. Anything that moves chat math somewhere useful works from that hidden semantic layer, not from the pixels on top.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
What Word stores
Word’s native equation format is OMML, Office Math Markup Language. An equation inside a .docx is a tree of m: elements in word/document.xml, in the namespace
http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math
Nothing on a web page produces OMML. That is the problem in one sentence.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
section: Route 1: linear format, typed by hand
text:
Route 1: linear format, typed by hand
Word accepts an equation written on one line and then “built up” into two dimensions. It supports two linear formats, and the difference matters: UnicodeMath, Microsoft’s own compact notation, and LaTeX.
Alt + = opens an equation field; type or paste the linear source; Ctrl + = builds it up. Ctrl + Shift + = goes back.
Two limits before you rely on it. Microsoft describes LaTeX input as new to Microsoft 365 subscribers, so on a perpetual licence do not assume it is there. And Word’s LaTeX is a dialect: \begin{} and \end{} are unsupported, so environments do not work and you write \matrix{a & b \\ c & d} instead, while \eqarray, \Middle, \ldiv and \dsmash are not supported at all.
This route works, it needs no tooling, and it does not scale past a few formulas.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
section: Route 2: hand Word its own format on the clipboard
text:
Route 2: hand Word its own format on the clipboard
This is the route that actually scales, and the one people are surprised exists.
When you paste into Word, Word does not read the plain-text flavour of the clipboard. It reads the text/html flavour — and it reads it as Word’s own HTML, a dialect that has carried Office-specific markup since the days of “Save as Web Page”. Word understands OMML embedded there, and it understands markup addressed to itself that every other application is required to skip.
That second property is what makes the whole thing work. A single clipboard payload can carry a real OMML equation for Word and readable LaTeX for everything else, and each reader takes its own branch. Paste into Word and you get a native equation; paste the same clipboard into a plain text editor and you get $\frac{RT}{V_m - b}$.
The practical consequence is that a tool doing this well is not “converting LaTeX to Word”. It is walking the page’s MathML into OMML, wrapping that in a Word-flavoured HTML payload, and writing text/html and text/plain together so the paste degrades sensibly wherever it lands. Getting the conversion right across real-world formulas — matrices, cases, multi-line alignments, over- and under-braces — is where the actual work is.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
Route 3: write the file
Skip the clipboard and generate the .docx yourself. A Word file is a zip of XML; the math goes in under the officeDocument/2006/math namespace and the document body under wordprocessingml/2006/main. Most work, most control, and the only route that handles a whole chat transcript at once rather than one formula at a time.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
section: Why Word on the web is different
text:
Why Word on the web is different
Word in a browser cannot accept a pasted equation from any application, because a browser tab never receives the rich clipboard payload the desktop app does. The conditional-comment trick needs Word itself reading the clipboard, and in the web app there is no Word reading the clipboard.
The workaround is Route 1, explicitly: Insert → Equation, paste the linear source into the box at the top of the panel, press Space, insert. It works, and it is also where the dialect limits bite hardest, because matrices, cases and multi-line equations are exactly what that box cannot build.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
PowerPoint, Excel, Google
One line in Microsoft’s documentation explains a great deal of confusion:

All other Office applications support only UnicodeMath.

PowerPoint, Excel and Outlook do not take LaTeX input. A workflow built on pasting LaTeX into Word does not transfer to a slide deck, which is why getting a formula into PowerPoint means OMML or an image.
Google Docs and Slides have no equation format worth targeting at all. There a high-resolution image is not a compromise, it is the correct answer.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
Picking a route









Route
Result
Where it works
Main cost




Linear, typed
Native, editable
Word desktop; LaTeX needs 365
Manual; dialect gaps


OMML in HTML clipboard
Native, editable
Word, PowerPoint desktop
Must generate OMML

Anywhere Word opens
Most work


Image
Not editable
Everywhere, incl. Google

There is no single format that is both easy to produce and universally accepted, which is the whole reason this is annoying.

title: Why AI Chat Math Won’t Paste Into Word, and What Actually Travels on the Clipboard
text:
The tool
I write thermodynamics, and a post like Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State carries over two hundred equations. Rebuilding those by hand in Word for a report was not something I was willing to keep doing, so I built TeXbridge, a Chrome and Edge extension that does the above: reads the hidden semantic layer, converts to OMML, and picks a target format based on where the formula is going. If a site renders something it handles badly, there is a support page and FAQ.
The mechanism is worth knowing either way. If you understand that the LaTeX is hiding in an annotation element, and that Word reads text/html with a conditional comment in it, you can get a formula where it needs to go by hand.

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
text:
\[
A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = \int_{V_R}^{V} \left( \frac{\partial A}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} dV = -\int_{V_R}^{V} P dV \tag{1}
\]
In Equation 1, the term \(V_R\) acts as an arbitrary reference volume, which corresponds to a specific but unknown reference Helmholtz free energy, \(A_R\) (where \(A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = A_R\)). To see how this plays out mathematically, let’s look at the most basic example using the ideal-gas equation of state:
\[
P^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) = \frac{n R_g T}{V} \tag{2}
\]
By substituting this into the fundamental volume derivative of the Helmholtz energy and performing the integration, we get:
\[
A^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) - A^{IG}(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = -\int_{V_R}^{V} P^{IG} dV
\]
\[
= -\int_{V_R}^{V} \frac{n R T}{V} dV = -n R_g T \ln\left(\frac{V}{V_R}\right) \tag{3}
\]
While Equation 3 allows us to calculate changes in Helmholtz free energy, it only provides the difference between states—we still do not know the absolute values of \(A\) or \(A_R\). If we differentiate Equation 3 with respect to temperature and apply the canonical entropy relationship, we arrive at a familiar expression for entropy:
\[
S^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) - S^{IG}(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = n R_g \ln\left(\frac{V}{V_R}\right) \tag{4}
\]
Notice that in Equation 4, the temperature remains constant between the state of interest and the reference state.
If we were to differentiate Equation 3 with respect to volume instead, we would simply get the ideal gas law (\(P = n R_g T / V\)). However, differentiating with respect to the number of moles yields the change in chemical potential:
\[
\mu_i^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) - \mu_i^{IG}(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = -R_g T \ln\left(\frac{V}{V_R}\right) \tag{5}
\]
These relationships highlight a major limitation: an equation of state (EOS) is not very helpful for calculating absolute thermodynamic properties. For instance, Equation 4 doesn’t give us the actual overarching formula for entropy; it only shows how entropy differences relate to changes in volume and composition. The same limitation applies to Equation 5 regarding chemical potential.
For now, we can set this limitation aside. Moving forward, we will apply this exact same mathematical framework to much more powerful equations of state. To make those models work, we will introduce the concept of a residual property—which is simply the mathematical difference between a property calculated from our advanced real-gas model and that same property calculated for an ideal gas.

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
text:
Soave–Redlich–Kwong Equation of State
Now, let’s apply the integration specified in Equation 3 to a more advanced model: the Soave-Redlich-Kwong equation of state (SRK EOS).
\[
P = \frac{n R_g T}{V - nb} - \frac{n^2 a}{V(V + nb)} \tag{6}
\]
In this expression, the parameters \(a\) and \(b\) are typically dependent on both temperature and composition. Notice that we have structured the SRK EOS here as a function of \(T\), \(V\), and the total number of moles (\(\bar{n}\)), rather than using mole fractions. We have also kept the unit choices generalized, consistent with our earlier discussions.
Finally, because it will be necessary for future calculations, we can determine the absolute minimum possible volume for the SRK EOS simply by inspecting the denominator of the first term:
\[
V_{min}^{SRK} = nb \tag{7}
\]
Before we dive into the integration, it helps to algebraically rewrite the SRK EOS into a form that is easier to integrate:
\[
P = \frac{n R_g T}{(V - nb)} - \frac{n^2 a}{nb} \left( \frac{1}{V} - \frac{1}{V + nb} \right) \tag{8}
\]
Applying the integration from Equation 3 to this new form yields:
\[
A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) = \left[ -n R_g T \ln(V - nb) + \frac{n^2 a}{nb} \ln \frac{V + nb}{V} \right]_{V_R}^{V}
\]
\[
= -n R_g T \ln \frac{(V - nb)}{(V_R - nb)} + \frac{n^2 a}{nb} \ln \frac{(V + nb)V_R}{V(V_R + nb)} \tag{9}
\]
At this point, we could try to push forward, but we run into the exact same roadblock we saw with Equation 3: we still don’t know the absolute value of \(A(T, V_R, \bar{n})\) for an SRK fluid at an arbitrary reference volume.
However, we can bypass this issue by comparing our SRK fluid calculations directly to those of an ideal gas. If we subtract the ideal gas result (Equation 3) from our SRK result (Equation 9), we get:
\[
A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) - A^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) + A^{IG}(T, V_R, \bar{n})
\]
\[
= -n R_g T \ln \frac{(V - nb)V_R}{(V_R - nb)V} + \frac{n^2 a}{nb} \ln \frac{(V + nb)V_R}{V(V_R + nb)} \tag{10}
\]
At first glance, it might look like we just mashed two underdefined equations together. But remember two crucial facts: first, the conditions \((T, V, V_R, \bar{n})\) apply equally to both the SRK fluid and the Ideal Gas. Second, we have complete freedom to choose our reference volume, \(V_R\), however is most convenient.
If we define \(V_R\) to approach infinity (\(V_R \to \infty\)), we are simulating an infinitely expanded gas. Because any valid, useful equation of state must trend toward ideal gas behavior at infinite volume, we can safely conclude that as \(V_R \to \infty\), the real fluid properties converge with the ideal gas properties (\(A(T, V_R, \bar{n}) \to A^{IG}(T, V_R, \bar{n})\)). Additionally, under this mathematical limit, terms like \(\frac{V_R}{V_R \pm nb}\) simply approach 1.






Note



As \(V_R \to \infty\), the \(nb\) term becomes negligible compared to the infinitely expanding volume, causing the fraction to approach unity:


\[
\lim_{V_R \to \infty} \frac{V_R}{V_R \pm nb} = 1 \tag{11}
\]
Alternatively, expressed as a simple directional trend:
\[
\frac{V_R}{V_R \pm nb} \to 1 \tag{12}
\]
By applying this infinite-volume reference state, Equation 10 beautifully simplifies to:
\[
A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) = -n R_g T \ln \left[ \frac{V - nb}{V} \right] + \frac{n^2 a}{nb} \ln \left[ \frac{V + nb}{V} \right] \tag{13}
\]
The left-hand side of Equation 13 provides us with the formal definition of the Residual Helmholtz Free Energy:
\[
A^{Res} \equiv A(T, V, \bar{n}) - A^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) \tag{14}
\]
It is crucial to understand the conceptual leap that led us to Equation 13, particularly how specific terms algebraically cancel out as our reference volume approaches infinity (\(V_R \to \infty\)). Furthermore, the core definition of any Residual Property strictly requires that both the real fluid and the Ideal Gas (IG) reference state share the exact same temperature (\(T\)), volume (\(V\)), and composition (\(\bar{n}\)). By substituting residual properties into our earlier definitions, we obtain the following relationships:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A^{Res}}{\partial T} \right)_{V, \bar{n}} = -S^{Res} = -S(T, V, \bar{n}) + S^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) \tag{15}
\]
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A^{Res}}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} = -P^{Res} = -P(T, V, \bar{n}) + \frac{n R_g T}{V} \tag{16}
\]
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A^{Res}}{\partial n_i} \right)_{T, V, n_{k \neq i}} = \mu_i^{Res} = \mu_i(T, V, \bar{n}) - \mu_i^{IG}(T, V, \bar{n}) \tag{17}
\]
However, Equations 15 through 17 do not magically solve all our problems. While we can differentiate Equation 13 with respect to \(T\), \(V\), or \(\bar{n}\) to generate residual properties, we still cannot determine the absolute property of the SRK fluid without knowing the corresponding property of the ideal gas.
Fortunately, we do know the pressure for both the ideal gas and the SRK fluid, which allows us to completely solve for the volume derivative, \(\left( \frac{\partial A^{Res}}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}}\).
Regarding composition (\(\bar{n}\)), we will see in the next section that if we can successfully formulate the ideal gas chemical potential (\(\mu_i^{IG}\)), we can then derive a highly useful expression for the chemical potential (\(\mu_i\)) of the SRK fluid (and other equations of state).
Finally, when it comes to temperature (\(T\)), we will discover that for a massive category of thermodynamic calculations, we actually do not need to know the absolute ideal gas entropy. In practice, those terms frequently end up canceling out algebraically when we assemble the final equations.

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
section: The Chemical Potential of an Ideal Gas
text:
The Chemical Potential of an Ideal Gas
Let’s start from the canonical derivative relation for the ideal gas Helmholtz free energy (Equation 18):
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A^{IG}}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} = -P^{IG} \tag{18}
\]
Substituting the ideal gas law, \(P^{IG} = \frac{n R_g T}{V}\) (Equation 2), yields:
\[
\left( \frac{\partial A^{IG}}{\partial V} \right)_{T, \bar{n}} = -\frac{n R_g T}{V} \tag{19}
\]
Integrating this expression with respect to volume (\(V\)), while keeping temperature (\(T\)) and the composition vector (\(\bar{n}\)) constant, gives us:
\[
A^{IG} = \int \left( -\frac{n R_g T}{V} \right) dV = -n R_g T \ln(V) + C \tag{20}
\]
In multivariable calculus, the “constant of integration” (\(C\)) is not simply a static number; it can depend on any variables that were deliberately held constant during the partial integration. Because \(T\) and \(\bar{n}\) were treated as constants, \(C\) is actually an arbitrary function, \(F(T, \bar{n})\). This leaves us with:
\[
A^{IG} = -n R_g T \ln(V) + F(T, \bar{n}) \tag{21}
\]

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
text:
Derivation of Equation 30
Equation 30 resolves the structure of this unknown integration function \(F(T, \bar{n})\) by leveraging Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions alongside the Legendre transform.

1. First Line of Equation 30: Euler Expansion of Helmholtz Energy
From classical thermodynamics, we know the fundamental potentials are related by:
\[
A \equiv U - TS = (H - PV) - TS = (H - TS) - PV = G - PV \tag{22}
\]
Applying Euler’s theorem for first-order extensive thermodynamic potentials tells us that the total Gibbs free energy is simply the sum of molar chemical potentials weighted by their respective mole numbers:
\[
G = \sum_r \mu_r n_r \tag{23}
\]
By substituting this definition of \(G\) back into our relation \(A = G - PV\) specifically for an ideal gas mixture, we arrive at the first line of Equation 30:
\[
A^{IG} = -(PV)^{IG} + \sum_r \mu_r^{IG} n_r \tag{24}
\]


2. Second Line of Equation 30: Matching the Volume and Composition Dependencies
Applying the ideal gas equation of state, we know that \((PV)^{IG} = n R_g T\). Substituting this into our previous expression yields:
\[
A^{IG} = -n R_g T + \sum_r \mu_r^{IG} n_r \tag{25}
\]
Recalling Equation 17, the chemical potential is defined as the partial derivative of the Helmholtz free energy with respect to the mole number:
\[
\mu_r^{IG} = \left( \frac{\partial A^{IG}}{\partial n_r} \right)_{T, V, n_{k \neq r}} \tag{26}
\]
Now, if we differentiate Equation 21 with respect to \(n_r\)—keeping in mind that the total moles \(n = \sum_j n_j\), meaning \(\frac{\partial n}{\partial n_r} = 1\)—we get:
\[
\mu_r^{IG} = -R_g T \ln(V) + \left( \frac{\partial F(T, \bar{n})}{\partial n_r} \right)_{T, n_{k \neq r}} \tag{27}
\]
To simplify this, we can define a dimensionless component function, \(f_r(T, \bar{n})\):
\[
f_r(T, \bar{n}) \equiv \frac{1}{R_g T} \left( \frac{\partial F}{\partial n_r} \right)_{T, n_{k \neq r}} \tag{28}
\]
This allows us to rewrite the chemical potential cleanly as:
\[
\mu_r^{IG} = R_g T \left[ -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \right] \tag{29}
\]
Finally, substituting this chemical potential back into our earlier expression (\(A^{IG} = -(PV)^{IG} + \sum_r \mu_r^{IG} n_r\)) brings us to the complete Equation 30:
\[
A^{IG} = -n R_g T + R_g T \sum_r \left[ -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \right] n_r \tag{30}
\]


1. The Extensivity Requirement (1st Order Homogeneity)
Helmholtz free energy (\(A\)) is fundamentally an extensive property. This means that if we scale the entire size of our system by some factor \(\lambda > 0\) while holding the temperature (\(T\)) constant, both the total volume (\(V\)) and the individual mole numbers (\(n_r\)) will scale by that exact same factor \(\lambda\):
\[
V \to \lambda V, \quad n_r \to \lambda n_r
\]
For the ideal gas Helmholtz energy (\(A^{IG}\)) to scale proportionally alongside the system (\(A^{IG} \to \lambda A^{IG}\)), it must mathematically behave as a function that is homogeneous of degree 1 with respect to volume and composition \((V, \bar{n})\).
Let’s look back at our newly derived Equation 30 to see how this applies:
\[
A^{IG} = -n R_g T + R_g T \sum_r \left[ -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \right] n_r
\]
The leading term, \(-n R_g T\), is naturally first-order homogeneous because the total moles scale directly with \(\lambda\) (where \(n = \sum n_r\), meaning \(n \to \lambda n\)).
Inside the summation, the trailing factor \(n_r\) also scales perfectly as \(\lambda^1\).
Because the \(n_r\) outside the brackets already satisfies the scaling requirement, the entire bracketed quantity, \(\left[ -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \right]\), must be homogeneous of degree 0. In other words, it must act as an intensive quantity that remains completely unchanged when the system is scaled by \(\lambda\):
\[
-\ln(\lambda V) + f_r(T, \lambda \bar{n}) = -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \tag{31}
\]
By expanding the logarithm on the left side of that relationship, we can isolate the function \(f_r\) to understand exactly how it must behave:
\[
-\ln(\lambda) - \ln(V) + f_r(T, \lambda \bar{n}) = -\ln(V) + f_r(T, \bar{n}) \tag{32}
\]
\[
f_r(T, \lambda \bar{n}) - f_r(T, \bar{n}) = \ln(\lambda) \tag{33}
\]


2. Derivation of Equation 37 via Euler’s Theorem
Euler’s homogeneous function theorem states that for any function \(g(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m)\) that is homogeneous of degree \(k\), the following relationship holds true:
\[
\sum_j x_j \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_j} = k \cdot g \tag{34}
\]
We can apply this theorem directly to our bracketed function, \(g(V, \bar{n}) = -\ln(V) + f_i(T, \bar{n})\), which we just established is homogeneous of degree zero (\(k = 0\)):
\[
V \frac{\partial \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right]}{\partial V} + \sum_r n_r \frac{\partial \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right]}{\partial n_r} = 0 \cdot \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right] = 0 \tag{35}
\]
Next, let’s quickly evaluate those two partial derivatives individually:

With respect to volume: \(\frac{\partial \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right]}{\partial V} = -\frac{1}{V}\)
With respect to mole numbers: \(\frac{\partial \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right]}{\partial n_r} = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial n_r}\)

Substituting these evaluated derivatives back into our Euler relation gives us the first line of Equation 37:
\[
-\frac{1}{V} V + \sum_r \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial n_r} n_r = 0 \tag{36}
\]
Finally, by simplifying the first term (\(-\frac{1}{V} V = -1\)) and moving that negative one to the right-hand side of the equation, we arrive perfectly at Equation 37:
\[
\sum_r \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial n_r} n_r = 1 \tag{37}
\]


1. Understanding the Behavior of \(f_i\)
Equation 37 reveals a couple of fascinating mathematical quirks about our component function, \(f_i\):

\(f_i\) is not homogeneous in \(\bar{n}\): Because the right-hand side of Equation 37 equals 1 rather than \(k \cdot f_i\), the function itself does not follow standard homogeneity rules.
Universal sum to 1 For that sum to reliably equal 1 regardless of the mixture’s actual composition, the partial derivative must perfectly isolate the specific component’s mole number. This means:

\[
\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial n_i} = \frac{1}{n_i} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial n_r} = 0 \quad (r \neq i) \tag{38}
\]
If we take that relationship and directly integrate \(\frac{1}{n_i} dn_i\), we arrive at Equation 39:
\[
f_i = \ln(n_i) + k_i(T) \tag{39}
\]
In this expression, \(k_i(T)\) serves as an integration constant that is exclusively dependent on the temperature, \(T\).


2. The Resulting Chemical Potential (Equation 40)
We are finally ready to put the pieces together. By substituting our newly derived \(f_i = \ln(n_i) + k_i\) back into the ideal gas chemical potential expression we built earlier (\(\mu_i^{IG} = R_g T \left[ -\ln(V) + f_i \right]\)), we get Equation 40:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = -R_g T \ln(V) + R_g T \ln(n_i) + R_g T k_i \tag{40}
\]
By algebraically grouping the volume and mole terms together, the underlying physics finally become visible. This arrangement reveals a direct, tangible connection to the molar concentration (\(c_i = n_i / V\)) or the partial pressure (\(P_i = y_i P\)):
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = R_g T \ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + R_g T k_i(T) \tag{41}
\]

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
text:
Determination of \(k_i\)

1. Matching \(\mu_i^{IG}\) to the Pure Component Limit
In Equation 40, the ideal gas chemical potential is given by:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = -R_g T \ln(V) + R_g T \ln(n_i) + R_g T k_i = R_g T \ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + R_g T k_i \tag{42}
\]
For a pure substance (\(n_i = n\)), the chemical potential is identical to the molar Gibbs free energy:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = g_i^{IG} \tag{43}
\]
Using the ideal gas relation (\(V = \frac{n R_g T}{P}\)), the molar concentration becomes \(\frac{n_i}{V} = \frac{P}{R_g T}\). Substituting this into Equation 42 gives us an expression for the pure ideal gas:
\[
g_i^{IG}(T, P) = R_g T \ln\left(\frac{P}{R_g T}\right) + R_g T k_i = R_g T \ln(P) - R_g T \ln(R_g T) + R_g T k_i \tag{44}
\]


2. Physical Origin of \(g_i^\circ(T)\) and Equation 48
To assign an actual numerical value to \(g_i^{IG}(T, P)\), thermodynamics anchors the property to standard formation data:
Reference State. Data for standard Gibbs energy of formation (\(\Delta g_{f, i}^\circ\)) or standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta h_{f, i}^\circ\)) and absolute entropy (\(s_i^\circ\)) are tabulated at \(T_0 = 298.15\text{ K}\) and \(P_0 = 1\text{ bar}\).
Temperature Integration. Using pure-component ideal-gas heat capacity polynomials (\(C_{p, i}^0(T)\)), the enthalpy and entropy are integrated from \(T_0\) to the system temperature \(T\):
\[
h_i^\circ(T) = \Delta h_{f, i}^\circ(T_0) + \int_{T_0}^T C_{p, i}^0(T') \, dT' \tag{45}
\]
\[
s_i^\circ(T) = s_i^\circ(T_0, P_0) + \int_{T_0}^T \frac{C_{p, i}^0(T')}{T'} \, dT' \tag{46}
\]
\[
g_i^\circ(T) \equiv h_i^\circ(T) - T s_i^\circ(T) = g_i(T, P_0) \tag{47}
\]
Pressure Isotherm (Equation 48). At a constant temperature, the change in Gibbs free energy with respect to pressure is given by \(dg_i = v \, dP = \frac{R_g T}{P} \, dP\). Integrating this from the standard pressure \(P_0\) to the system pressure \(P\) gives:
\[
g_i^{IG}(T, P) = g_i(T, P_0) + R_g T \ln\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) = g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \ln(P) - R_g T \ln(P_0) \tag{48}
\]


3. Solving Explicitly for \(k_i(T)\)
We now have two different expressions for \(g_i^{IG}(T, P)\). Equating them directly isolates our unknown integration constant, \(k_i(T)\):
\[
R_g T \ln(P) - R_g T \ln(R_g T) + R_g T k_i = g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \ln(P) - R_g T \ln(P_0) \tag{49}
\]
Notice that the \(R_g T \ln(P)\) term beautifully cancels out on both sides:
\[
-R_g T \ln(R_g T) + R_g T k_i = g_i^\circ(T) - R_g T \ln(P_0) \tag{50}
\]
Finally, by dividing everything through by \(R_g T\), we arrive at our explicit solution for the temperature-dependent integration constant:
\[
k_i(T) = \frac{g_i^\circ(T)}{R_g T} + \ln\left(\frac{R_g T}{P_0}\right) \tag{51}
\]
Let’s start by revisiting Equation 40 and factoring out the \(R_g T\) term:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = -R_g T \ln(V) + R_g T \ln(n_i) + R_g T k_i \tag{52}
\]
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = R_g T \left[ \ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + k_i(T) \right] \tag{53}
\]
From our previous derivation (Equation 51), we solved for the explicit expression of \(k_i(T)\):
\[
k_i(T) = \frac{g_i^\circ(T)}{R_g T} + \ln(R_g T) - \ln(P_0) \tag{54}
\]


Step 2: Substitution of \(k_i(T)\)
Now, we substitute that expression for \(k_i(T)\) directly into our bracketed term:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = R_g T \left[ \ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + \frac{g_i^\circ(T)}{R_g T} + \ln(R_g T) - \ln(P_0) \right] \tag{55}
\]
By distributing \(R_g T\) back through the equation, we can pull the standard Gibbs energy out front:
\[
\mu_i^{IG} = g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \left[ \ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + \ln(R_g T) - \ln(P_0) \right] \tag{56}
\]


Step 3: Combining the Logarithmic Terms
Using standard logarithmic identities (\(\ln(x) + \ln(y) = \ln(xy)\) and \(\ln(a) - \ln(b) = \ln(a/b)\)), we can compress the terms inside the bracket:
\[
\ln\left(\frac{n_i}{V}\right) + \ln(R_g T) - \ln(P_0) = \ln\left( \frac{n_i R_g T}{V \cdot P_0} \right) \tag{57}
\]
Next, we express the total mixture pressure using the ideal gas law (\(P = \frac{n R_g T}{V}\)), which rearranges to \(\frac{R_g T}{V} = \frac{P}{n}\). Substituting this into our logarithmic argument simplifies it beautifully:
\[
\frac{n_i R_g T}{V \cdot P_0} = \frac{n_i}{n} \cdot \frac{P}{P_0} \tag{59}
\]


Step 4: The Final Form of Equation 61
Let \(c_i \equiv y_i = \frac{n_i}{n}\) represent the mole fraction of species \(i\) in our ideal gas mixture. We can split the product inside the logarithm one last time:
\[
\ln\left( \frac{P}{P_0} \cdot c_i \right) = \ln\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) + \ln(c_i) \tag{60}
\]
Multiplying this by \(R_g T\) and adding it back to \(g_i^\circ(T)\) yields the final, highly useful Equation 61:
\[
\mu_i^{IG}(T, P, \bar{n}) = g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \ln\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) + R_g T \ln(c_i) \tag{61}
\]

title: Thermodynamic Potentials Applied for Equations of State
text:
Physical Interpretation and Real-Fluid Extension
Equation 61 is incredibly elegant because every single term tells a specific physical story about the gas:

Reference State (\(g_i^\circ\)) This captures the pure substance’s caloric properties at temperature \(T\) and standard pressure \(P_0\) (typically 1 bar).
Isothermal Pressure Effect (\(R_g T \ln(P/P_0)\)) This mathematically compresses or expands the pure ideal gas isothermally from standard pressure to the actual system pressure \(P\).
Ideal Mixing Effect (\(R_g T \ln c_i\)) This accounts for the entropy of mixing at constant temperature and pressure, representing Dalton’s partial pressure contribution.

For a real fluid, we simply add the residual chemical potential (\(\mu_i^{Res} = \left(\frac{\partial A^{Res}}{\partial n_i}\right)_{T, V, n_{k \neq i}}\)) to define the total chemical potential:
\[
\mu_i = \mu_i^{IG} + \mu_i^{Res} = g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \ln\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) + R_g T \ln(c_i) + \mu_i^{Res} \tag{62}
\]
Because the chemical potential of a real component is formally defined via its fugacity (\(\hat{f}_i\)) as:
\[
\mu_i \equiv g_i^\circ(T) + R_g T \ln\left(\frac{\hat{f}_i}{P_0}\right) \tag{63}
\]
We can equate the two forms. By defining the fugacity coefficient as \(\phi_i \equiv \frac{\hat{f}_i}{c_i P}\), we directly recover the fundamental link between residual properties and phase equilibrium:
\[
\ln \phi_i = \frac{\mu_i^{Res}}{R_g T} - \ln Z \tag{64}
\]






Note



The \(\ln Z\) term, where compressibility factor \(Z = \frac{PV}{n R_g T}\), acts as the required mathematical adjustment for the coordinate transformation from the \((T, V)\) Helmholtz domain over to the \((T, P)\) Gibbs domain).
